chapter_title: Writing Unit Tests with Hardhat & Waffle

screens.title: Writing Unit Tests with Hardhat & Waffle
screens.subtitle: Use Hardhat, ethers.js and Waffle to make Solidity contracts reliable

narration.text: In this lesson we will learn how to write unit tests for Solidity contracts using Hardhat and Waffle. You will see how test files are structured with describe, it, and beforeEach, how to deploy contracts inside tests with ethers. js, and how to assert both success and failure cases using Waffle matchers. Testing is more than verifying happy paths: it documents expected behavior, catches regressions early, and gives you confidence when changing code. For example, a simple Counter contract should have tests that check initial state, increments, decrements, and that a require condition reverts with the correct message. Throughout this chapter we’ll walk through those patterns, explain common mistakes like forgetting await or not resetting state, and give you practical starter tasks for a Storage contract. By the end you’ll know how to deploy contracts inside beforeEach, get signers to simulate different accounts, and write assertions for state changes and reverts. Ready to build reliable smart contracts and reduce surprises during deployment?

keyIdea.title: Core message
keyIdea.text: Tests isolate behavior with beforeEach, interact via ethers.js signers, and assert outcomes with Waffle matchers so contracts behave as intended.

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to write basic unit tests for individual Solidity functions using Hardhat and Waffle, and you will understand how to structure test files so they are maintainable. You will learn to use common Waffle assertion methods to verify both successful state changes and expected reverts, which helps capture edge cases. The chapter also teaches how to deploy contracts into the test environment using ethers. getContractFactory, wait for deployment with deployed(), and get signers via ethers. getSigners to simulate different accounts. Finally, you will practice writing tests that use beforeEach to reset state and ensure isolation between tests. Each objective pairs a practical task with why it matters: isolated tests make failures diagnosable, correct assertions prevent silent bugs, and signer management validates access control scenarios. These competencies translate directly into safer, more trustworthy smart contracts.

screens.title: Test File Structure: describe, it, beforeEach
screens.subtitle: Organize tests so they read like a specification

narration.text: A Hardhat test file follows a clear structure built from describe, it, and beforeEach. The describe block groups related tests, typically for one contract or a single feature set. Inside describe, each it block defines an individual test case that states a single expected behavior. The beforeEach hook is a setup routine that runs before every it in its scope. Use it to deploy a fresh contract instance and to set initial state so tests don’t share mutated state. For example, a describe for Counter contains it tests for initial value, increment, decrement, and revert behavior. Placing deployment in beforeEach ensures each it starts with count equal to zero. A common misconception is using before to deploy once for all tests; this can make tests order-dependent and flaky. Think of beforeEach as re-creating a clean sandbox before every assertion, so tests remain predictable and easy to debug. When writing suites, prefer small, focused it blocks and move repeated setup into beforeEach to keep tests concise and maintainable. What behavior will your next it describe? Test File Structure: describe, it, beforeEach means use describe to group tests, it for single expectations, and beforeeach to reset state for isolation.. In practical terms, organize tests so they read like a specification. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Structure rule
keyIdea.text: Use describe to group tests, it for single expectations, and beforeEach to reset state for isolation.

content.html:
Core Concept
describe, it, beforeEach
A disciplined structure keeps tests readable and isolated.
describe()
Groups related tests for one contract or feature.
it()
An individual test case describing expected behavior.
beforeEach()
Runs setup before every it to ensure clean state.
Concrete example
A beforeEach deploys Counter so each it sees count reset to zero, avoiding test interdependence.
Key Takeaway

Keep tests atomic: one expectation per it, clean state via beforeEach, and group with describe for clarity.

Typical pattern (annotated)
// test/Counter.js
describe("Counter", function () {
  let Counter;
  let counter;
  let owner;

  beforeEach(async function () {
    Counter = await ethers.getContractFactory("Counter");
    [owner] = await ethers.getSigners();
    counter = await Counter.deploy();
    await counter.deployed();
  });

  it("Should have an initial count of 0", async function () {
    expect(await counter.getCount()).to.equal(0);
  });
});
Common mistake
Using before instead of beforeEach can leave mutated state between tests and produce order-dependent failures.

narration.text: Deploying within tests uses a short sequence of steps. First, call ethers. getContractFactory with your contract name to obtain a ContractFactory. Next, request test accounts with ethers. getSigners which returns Signer objects that simulate real accounts. Use the ContractFactory to call deploy(), which returns a Contract instance wrapped in a Promise; await that promise. Then call await deployed() to ensure the deployment transaction is mined and the contract address is available. This sequence belongs inside beforeEach so every test works with a pristine contract. A concrete case: for Counter, getContractFactory("Counter"), destructure two signers as owner and addr1, then call Counter. deploy() and await counter. deployed(). A common misconception is thinking deploy() is synchronous; forgetting await leaves you with unresolved promises and unpredictable test behavior. Also be mindful that getSigners returns in-memory accounts only in the Hardhat Network, not external nodes. By following the process, your test suite will reliably deploy and interact with contracts for assertions and multi-account scenarios. Deploying Contracts in Tests means factory → signers → deploy() → await deployed() inside beforeeach ensures stable test setup.. In practical terms, ethers.getcontractfactory, getsigners, deploy, deployed. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Deployment steps
keyIdea.text: Factory → Signers → deploy() → await deployed() inside beforeEach ensures stable test setup.

content.html:
Process Flow
Deploying Contracts in Tests
1
Get ContractFactory
ethers.getContractFactory('YourContract')
2
Get Signers
const [owner, addr1] = await ethers.getSigners()
3
Deploy and await
const c = await Factory.deploy(); await c.deployed()
Example note
Place these steps inside beforeEach to ensure each test begins with a newly deployed contract instance and known signer roles.
Common mistake
Forgetting to await deploy() or deployed() leaves unresolved promises and can cause assertions to run before the contract exists.
Try this
beforeEach(async function () {
  const Factory = await ethers.getContractFactory("Counter");
  [owner, addr1] = await ethers.getSigners();
  counter = await Factory.deploy();
  await counter.deployed();
});
Key Takeaway

Always await asynchronous deployment steps and run them in beforeEach for isolation.

screens.title: Counter Example: Tests That Assert State Changes
screens.subtitle: Increment, decrement, and initial state assertions

narration.text: Let’s step through a concrete Counter test suite. The suite first deploys the Counter in beforeEach, then checks the initial count equals zero using expect(await counter. getCount()). to. equal(0). The increment test sends a transaction by awaiting counter. increment() and then asserts the returned count equals one. For decrement, the test increments first to ensure the count is greater than zero, then calls decrement and asserts the count returns to zero. The revert case tests the require condition: when decrement is called from zero, the test expects the call to be reverted with the message 'Count cannot be negative' using expect(...). to. be. revertedWith. Finally, a test demonstrates signer usage by connecting addr1 with counter. connect(addr1). increment() to verify another account can change state. A frequent mistake is over-asserting multiple unrelated properties in a single it, which makes failures harder to interpret. Keep tests focused: one behavior per it, and use clear assertions for state and revert messages so your suite documents contract intents. Counter Example: Tests That Assert State Changes means assert initial state, test state-changing methods, and verify reverts with exact messages for clarity.. In practical terms, increment, decrement, and initial state assertions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Test pattern
keyIdea.text: Assert initial state, test state-changing methods, and verify reverts with exact messages for clarity.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Counter test file
// test/Counter.js
const { expect } = require("chai");
const { ethers } = require("hardhat");

describe("Counter", function () {
  let Counter;
  let counter;
  let owner;
  let addr1;

  beforeEach(async function () {
    Counter = await ethers.getContractFactory("Counter");
    [owner, addr1] = await ethers.getSigners();
    counter = await Counter.deploy();
    await counter.deployed();
  });

  it("Should have an initial count of 0", async function () {
    expect(await counter.getCount()).to.equal(0);
  });

  it("Should increment the count by 1", async function () {
    await counter.increment();
    expect(await counter.getCount()).to.equal(1);
  });

  it("Should revert if decrementing from zero", async function () {
    await expect(counter.decrement()).to.be.revertedWith("Count cannot be negative");
  });

  it("Should allow other accounts to increment", async function () {
    await counter.connect(addr1).increment();
    expect(await counter.getCount()).to.equal(1);
  });
});
Explanation points
  • Initial state test confirms constructor behavior.
  • State-changing functions require awaiting the transaction before asserting.
  • revertedWith checks specific error messages from require.
  • connect(signer) simulates calls from different accounts for access testing.
Key Takeaway

Write focused tests that validate one behavior and one assertion per it. Use revert checks for error paths.

screens.title: Assertions: to.equal vs to.be.revertedWith
screens.subtitle: Check values and error conditions with Waffle matchers

narration.text: Waffle matchers extend Chai with domain-specific assertions for Ethereum. The two most common forms in unit tests are to. equal and to. be. revertedWith. Use to. equal to compare values returned by view functions or to verify the state after a transaction. For example, expect(await counter. getCount()). to. equal(1) confirms that a state change occurred. Use to. be. revertedWith when you expect a transaction to fail due to a require or revert. That matcher checks the failure and verifies the revert string, which ensures the contract is rejecting the operation for the expected reason. A misconception is treating revertedWith as optional; without checking the message you may accept any revert reason and miss incorrect error handling. Another pitfall is asserting the wrong data type: to. equal expects comparable primitive values. For stateful checks following a transaction, always re-query the contract with await and assert the returned value. Combining both matchers in a suite covers happy and unhappy paths, giving robust documentation of intended contract behavior. Assertions: to.equal vs to.be.revertedWith means use to.equal for state checks and to.be.revertedwith for expected failure messages to fully describe behavior.. In practical terms, check values and error conditions with waffle matchers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Assertion rule
keyIdea.text: Use to.equal for state checks and to.be.revertedWith for expected failure messages to fully describe behavior.

content.html:
Comparison
to.equal vs to.be.revertedWith
to.equal
Compare returned values or state after a transaction. Always await the view call.
to.be.revertedWith
Assert a transaction fails and includes the expected revert message from require or revert.
Examples
expect(await counter.getCount()).to.equal(1);
await expect(counter.decrement()).to.be.revertedWith("Count cannot be negative");
Why both matter
  • Value assertions confirm side effects and return values.
  • Revert assertions confirm guards and error handling.
  • Together, they describe both correct and safe failure behaviors.
Key Takeaway

Assert both success and failure paths with precise matchers to make tests meaningful documentation.

screens.title: Using Signers and connect() to Simulate Accounts
screens.subtitle: Test multi-user behavior and msg.sender-dependent logic

narration.text: Signers represent accounts in the Hardhat test environment. When you call const [owner, addr1] = await ethers. getSigners(), you receive Signer objects that can send transactions. To simulate a transaction from a different account, use contract. connect(signer). method(). For instance, counter. connect(addr1). increment() sends the increment transaction from addr1, not the original deployer. This is essential when testing functions that depend on msg. sender, such as owner-only actions or permission checks. A common pitfall is assuming all transactions come from the deployer; without explicit connect calls, calls will be made from the default signer used to create the contract object. Another useful pattern is naming signers clearly—owner, user, attacker—so tests communicate intent. When testing access controls like updateOwner in Storage, attempt the call both from owner and from addr1 to confirm only the owner can update. Use expect(...). to. be. revertedWith for the unauthorized case. Signers let you cover role-based scenarios and surface permission bugs before deployment. Using Signers and connect() to Simulate Accounts means use ethers.getsigners and contract.connect(signer) to model different actors and test msg.sender-dependent logic.. In practical terms, test multi-user behavior and msg.sender-dependent logic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Signer usage
keyIdea.text: Use ethers.getSigners and contract.connect(signer) to model different actors and test msg.sender-dependent logic.

content.html:
Technique
Signers & connect()
Use getSigners to obtain accounts, then contract.connect(signer) to send transactions from that account. This is how you test owner-only functions and multi-user interactions. 
const [owner, user] = await ethers.getSigners();
await contract.connect(user).someAction();
Concrete scenario
Test updateOwner by calling updateOwner(newAddr) from owner and from a non-owner. The non-owner call should revert with the owner-only require message.
Key Takeaway

Explicitly connect the signer you intend to simulate to avoid mistaken assumptions about msg.sender.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
screens.subtitle: Forgetting await, not resetting state, signer mistakes, and over-asserting

narration.text: There are a few recurring mistakes when writing Hardhat tests. First, forgetting await on asynchronous calls like deploy(), deployed(), or transactions leads to race conditions and assertion errors because the test continues before the Promise resolves. Always await contract interactions. Second, not resetting state across tests causes flaky suites: if you deploy once for all tests, one test may change state and break later tests. Use beforeEach to re-deploy. Third, incorrect signer usage means you may test with the wrong msg. sender; use contract. connect(signer) to make intentions explicit. Fourth, over-asserting—checking too many unrelated properties in a single it—makes failures harder to diagnose. Keep one assertion or one small related set of assertions per it. Finally, mismatched revert messages or checking for generic reverts without the message can mask incorrect error handling. Write clear, focused tests and avoid these pitfalls to build reliable, maintainable test suites. Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them means await promises, reset state per test, connect correct signer, and keep tests focused to prevent flakiness.. In practical terms, forgetting await, not resetting state, signer mistakes, and over-asserting. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Avoid traps
keyIdea.text: Await promises, reset state per test, connect correct signer, and keep tests focused to prevent flakiness.

content.html:
Best Practice
Common Mistakes and Fixes
Forgetting await
Always await deploy(), transactions, and view calls when needed.
Not resetting state
Use beforeEach to redeploy and avoid test interdependence.
Incorrect signer
Explicitly connect the intended signer for msg.sender checks.
Over-asserting
One behavior per it keeps failures meaningful and debugging fast.
Key Takeaway

Follow clear async patterns, isolate tests, and simulate the correct actors to keep suites reliable.

screens.title: Storage Contract Activity — Starter Code
screens.subtitle: Write tests for Storage.sol: initial value, store, retrieve, updateOwner

narration.text: The hands-on activity asks you to write tests for Storage. sol. The contract stores a private uint value, emits ValueChanged on store, and allows only the owner to updateOwner. Start by deploying Storage in beforeEach and assert the initial _value is zero and owner equals the deployer address. For store, call store(newValue), await the transaction, then assert retrieve() returns newValue and the ValueChanged event was emitted with the correct old and new values. For updateOwner, write three tests: owner updates owner successfully, a non-owner call reverts with the owner-only message, and setting the zero address reverts with the expected message. Each test should focus on one behavior. As a bonus, assert the event emission using Waffle’s event helpers or by checking the transaction receipt. This exercise ties together deployment, signers, state assertions, event checks, and revert expectations to build test-writing fluency. Unit Test a Simple Storage Contract
Starter code and tests should live under contracts/ and test/. The test tasks include verifying initial state, owner, store, retrieve, and updateOwner edge cases including zero address and non-owner calls.
Starter test skeleton
const { expect } = require("chai");
const { ethers } = require("hardhat");

describe("Storage", function () {
  let Storage;
  let storage;
  let owner;
  let addr1;

  beforeEach(async function () {
    Storage = await ethers.getContractFactory("Storage");
    [owner, addr1] = await ethers.getSigners();
    storage = await Storage.deploy();
    await storage.deployed();
  });

  // TODO: write tests per activity instructions
});
Tasks
  1. Test initial _value is 0.
  2. Test owner is deployer.
  3. Test store updates the value and emits ValueChanged.
  4. Test retrieve returns stored value.

screens.title: Testing Reverts: Example Withdrawal Test
screens.subtitle: Verify a function reverts with the expected message when conditions fail

narration.text: The assessment asks you to write a test that confirms a withdraw function reverts when the requested amount exceeds the sender’s balance. The test sets up a contract with an initial balance mapping for the owner of one hundred, then attempts to withdraw two hundred. The expected behavior is a revert with the message 'Insufficient balance'. To test this, use expect(contract. connect(owner). withdraw(200)). to. be. revertedWith("Insufficient balance"). Before asserting the revert, ensure the initial balance is correctly set in the test setup. A misconception is to check for a generic revert without the message; that will not validate the specific guard condition. After the revert assertion, also verify the balance remains unchanged to ensure no side effects occurred. This pattern checks both the failure path and its invariants, which is useful for preventing financial bugs in contracts that handle funds or balances. Testing Reverts: Example Withdrawal Test means arrange initial balances, act with an overdraw, and assert revertedwith the exact message and unchanged state.. In practical terms, verify a function reverts with the expected message when conditions fail. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Arrange initial balances, act with an overdraw, and assert revertedWith the exact message and unchanged state.

Verify withdraw reverts on insufficient balance
Arrange a contract state with balances[msg.sender] equal to 100, then attempt withdraw(200) and assert the call reverts with the message "Insufficient balance". Finally, re-check the balance is unchanged.
await expect(myContract.connect(owner).withdraw(200))
  .to.be.revertedWith("Insufficient balance");

screens.title: Live Coding and Test Iteration
screens.subtitle: Run npx hardhat test, fix failing assertions, and re-run quickly

narration.text: A productive workflow is: write a focused test, run it with npx hardhat test, inspect failures, fix the contract or test, and repeat. Running a single test file accelerates iteration. When tests fail, read the revert message and the assertion mismatch to locate the root cause. If a require triggers, check the preconditions you intended in beforeEach. If a value differs, print the returned value in the test flow or examine the transaction receipt for events. The live-coding plan in this chapter walks through Counter. sol and test/Counter. js: you’ll intentionally break a require to see the failed test, then restore it and watch tests pass. Keep tests small so you can run them often. A common misconception is running the entire suite for every minor change; prefer targeted runs and incremental fixes. This iterative loop — write, run, diagnose, fix — is the fastest path to a stable suite and clearer contract semantics. Live Coding and Test Iteration means write focused tests and run them repeatedly with targeted runs to diagnose and fix failures efficiently.. In practical terms, run npx hardhat test, fix failing assertions, and re-run quickly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Iterative cycle

screens.title: Putting It Together: Test Strategy Checklist
screens.subtitle: A short checklist to keep your test suite healthy

narration.text: Before finishing a test suite or pushing changes, run through a short checklist. First, ensure each it tests one clear behavior and uses focused assertions. Second, verify you deploy in beforeEach so tests remain isolated and reproducible. Third, confirm you await asynchronous operations like deploy() and transactions before asserting state changes. Fourth, check signer usage: use contract. connect(signer) for each actor role you intend to simulate. Fifth, assert both the happy path with to. equal and unhappy paths with to. be. revertedWith including the revert message. Sixth, include event assertions for functions that emit events so behavior is observable in transaction receipts. Finally, run targeted test files during iteration and run the full suite in CI. This checklist helps maintain a fast, stable suite that documents intended behavior and prevents regressions during refactors or audits. Putting It Together: Test Strategy Checklist means one-behavior-per-test, beforeeach deployment, await async calls, explicit signers, assert success and failures, and include event checks.. In practical terms, a short checklist to keep your test suite healthy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Checklist
keyIdea.text: One-behavior-per-test, beforeEach deployment, await async calls, explicit signers, assert success and failures, and include event checks.

Wrap-up
Test Strategy Checklist
  • One focused behavior per it.
  • Use beforeEach for clean deploys.
  • Always await async operations.
  • Explicitly connect signers for role tests.
  • Assert values and revert messages.
  • Test event emissions for important state changes.
  • Run targeted tests while iterating.
  • Include suite execution in CI.
Key Takeaway

A small disciplined checklist ensures tests scale with code changes and remain trustworthy documentation of behavior.

Use Waffle matchers to assert correct return values with to. equal and to verify expected failures with to. be. revertedWith. screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders to carry forward

narration.text: Keep three quick reminders in mind as you write tests. First, isolate tests by deploying in beforeEach so each it runs on a fresh instance. Second, simulate roles with ethers. getSigners and contract. connect to verify access control and multi-user flows. Third, assert both expected state changes and expected failures: use to. equal for values and to. be. revertedWith for required error messages. These three practices cover most unit testing needs for small to medium Solidity projects and will make your test suite easier to maintain and more trustworthy when you audit or refactor code. Key Concepts — Quick Reference means isolate tests, simulate accounts, and assert success and failure precisely.. In practical terms, three compact reminders to carry forward. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Quick Reference
Isolate tests
Use beforeEach to redeploy.
Simulate accounts
Use getSigners and connect(signer).
Assert precisely
Check values and exact revert messages.
Summary

Run focused, isolated tests that cover happy and unhappy paths to keep contracts robust and auditable.
